title: Kindness Rules from the Rabbis
bigQuestion: What kindness rules did the rabbis write down, and who does each rule help?

story.title: The Lost Mitten
story.kicker: One red mitten in the snow, and a whole class decides what to do about it.
paragraphs: It is a cold day in Chicago. Recess is over. Jada finds a red mitten in the snow. It is not hers. It has a small yellow star on it. She holds it up. "Whose is this?" Nobody answers.
Back inside, the class talks about it. Ben says, "Finders keepers." Jada shakes her head. "Somebody's hand is cold right now." Mr. Ortiz asks, "So what should a finder do?"

The class makes a rule. A finder does not keep it. A finder puts it in the Lost Box. A finder says what it looks like, but not everything. The owner has to say the secret part. "Mine has a yellow star," someone would say.

Mr. Ortiz smiles. "You just did what the rabbis did," he says. "They asked the same question. They wrote their answer in a book called the Talmud. This week, we will read some of their kindness rules."
story.think: Why did the class say the owner has to tell the secret part of the mitten? What would go wrong without that rule?

lessons.title: Visiting the Sick
lessons.mainIdea: The rabbis said visiting a sick person is a mitzvah, and it makes them feel better.
reading: A rule in the Torah is called a *mitzvah*. The rabbis found many mitzvot about being kind. One is visiting someone who is sick. The Hebrew name is bikkur cholim.
The Talmud tells why. It says God visited Abraham when he was hurting. The rabbis read that as a lesson. If God visits the sick, people should too.
The Talmud also says a visit helps. One rabbi said a visit takes away a bit of the sickness. A sick person is not alone. That feels better.

words.d: a rule in the Torah; the rabbis also use it for a good deed; more than one is mitzvot
visiting the sick, a mitzvah the rabbis talked about in the Talmud

look.title: Why Visit?
look.text: The Talmud says: Just as God visited the sick, when God came to Abraham after he was hurt, so you should visit the sick.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Sotah 14a, retold in simple words; the verse is Genesis 18:1
look.prompt: The rabbis read a story about Abraham as a rule for everyone. What is the rule?

check.q: What is a mitzvah?
check.why: A mitzvah is a rule in the Torah. The rabbis also use the word for a good deed.

check.q: Who did the Talmud say God visited?
check.why: The Talmud (Sotah 14a) says God visited Abraham after he was hurt.

check.q: What does bikkur cholim mean?
check.why: Bikkur cholim is the Hebrew name for visiting the sick.

lessons.title: Welcoming a Guest
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah says Abraham ran to feed three strangers, and the rabbis made that a rule.
reading: The Torah tells a story about Abraham. He sat by his tent on a hot day. Three strangers walked by. Abraham ran to them. He asked them to rest. He brought water and bread. He served a big meal.
The rabbis loved this story. They said welcoming a *guest* is a great mitzvah. The Hebrew name is hachnasat orchim. That means bringing in guests.
The Talmud says something big about it. It says welcoming guests is even greater than greeting God. Why? Because Abraham left God's presence to run to the strangers. The rabbis read that as a lesson.

words.d: a person who comes to your home or table; the rabbis said to welcome guests warmly
bringing in guests; the rabbis' name for the mitzvah of welcoming people

look.title: Abraham's Meal
rows: Measures of flour for the bread
look.prompt: Abraham made a very big meal for three people. What does that tell you about how he treated guests?

check.q: What did Abraham do when he saw the strangers?
check.why: Genesis 18 says Abraham ran to meet the strangers and fed them.

check.q: What does hachnasat orchim mean?
check.why: Hachnasat orchim means bringing in guests. It is the mitzvah of welcoming.

check.q: Which book tells the story of Abraham's guests?
check.why: The story is in Genesis 18, the first book of the Torah.

lessons.title: Honoring Parents
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah says honor your father and mother, and the Talmud tells how.
reading: One of the Ten Commandments is about parents. The Torah says: honor your father and your mother. The rabbis asked, what does *honor* mean? What do you actually do?
The Talmud gives a list. You help them eat. You help them dress. You help them get around. You speak to them with respect.

The Talmud also tells a story. A man named Dama had a rare stone to sell. Buyers offered a lot of money. But the key was under his sleeping father's pillow. Dama would not wake him. He lost the sale. The rabbis said that is honor.

words.d: to treat someone with respect and care; the Torah tells children to honor their parents

look.title: The Commandment
look.text: Honour thy father and thy mother, that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.
look.prompt: This is old English. Say it in your own words. What does it tell a child to do?

check.q: Which commandment is this lesson about?
check.why: The lesson is about the commandment to honor your father and mother (Exodus 20:12).

check.q: Why did Dama lose the sale?
choices: He would not wake his father
check.why: The Talmud (Kiddushin 31a) says the key was under his sleeping father's pillow, and Dama would not wake him.

check.q: What is one way the Talmud says to honor parents?
check.why: The Talmud lists helping parents eat, dress and get around as ways to honor them.

lessons.title: Do Not Shame Anyone
lessons.mainIdea: The rabbis said shaming someone in front of others hurts as much as a wound.
reading: Words can hurt. The rabbis knew this. The Talmud says do not *shame* a person in front of others. Shame is when someone feels small and everyone sees.
The Talmud says a shamed person's face turns white. The rabbis compared that to a wound. They said it is a very serious thing to do.
The rabbis even said this. It is better to be thrown into a fire than to shame someone in public. That is a strong way to talk. It shows how much the rule mattered to them.

words.d: to make someone feel small in front of others; the rabbis said never to do it

look.title: At the Lunch Table
look.text: Look at the lunch table. Sam spills milk on his shirt. Everyone is watching. One kid points and laughs loudly. Another kid hands Sam a napkin and starts talking about the game at recess. Sam's face was red. Now it is not.
look.prompt: Which kid followed the rabbis' rule about shame? What did that kid do to help?

check.q: What does the Talmud say not to do in public?
check.why: The Talmud (Bava Metzia 58b) says not to shame a person in front of others.

check.q: What did the rabbis compare shaming to?
check.why: The rabbis said a shamed person's face goes white, like a wound.

check.q: What is shame?
check.why: Shame is feeling small in front of others. The rabbis said never to cause it.

lessons.title: Returning Lost Things
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah says bring a lost thing back, and the Mishnah says how to find the owner.
reading: The Torah has a rule about lost things. If you see your neighbor's lost animal, do not walk past. Bring it back. The rabbis read this for all lost things.
The Mishnah asks how. A finder says out loud what was found. The owner gives a *sign*. A sign is a secret detail only the owner knows. If the sign matches, the thing goes home.
That is like the class rule about the mitten. The finder says: a red mitten. The owner says: with a yellow star. The rabbis wrote this in a tractate called Bava Metzia.

words.d: a secret detail that shows a lost thing is really yours
a tractate of the Talmud about lost things, buying, selling and being fair; the name means the middle gate

look.title: Do Not Walk Past
look.text: The Torah says: If you see your neighbor's ox or sheep wandering, do not hide and pretend you did not see. Bring it back to your neighbor.
look.cite: Deuteronomy 22:1, retold in simple words from the Jewish Publication Society translation, 1917
look.prompt: The verse talks about an ox and a sheep. What else could the rule be about today?

check.q: What is a sign, in the Mishnah's rule?
choices: A secret detail only the owner knows
check.why: A sign is a secret detail. The owner gives it, and it shows the thing is theirs.

check.q: What does the Torah say to do with a lost animal?
check.why: Deuteronomy 22:1 says not to hide from it, but to bring it back.

check.q: Which tractate has the rules for lost things?
check.why: Bava Metzia, the middle gate, has the rules about lost things.

lessons.title: A Share for Those in Need
lessons.mainIdea: Tzedakah is giving a share to people who need it, and the rabbis said everyone gives.
reading: The Torah tells farmers to leave the corners of a field. Poor people come and take what grows there. The rabbis made a bigger rule from this. It is called *tzedakah*.
Tzedakah means giving a share to people who need it. The word comes from a word for fair. The rabbis said it is not extra. It is what is fair.
The Talmud says even a poor person gives tzedakah. Everyone has something to give. Later, a rabbi named Maimonides made a ladder of giving. The best step is helping someone earn their own.

words.d: giving a share to people who need it; the word comes from a word for fair

look.title: The Ladder of Giving
rows: Steps on Maimonides's ladder of giving
Best step: helping someone earn their own
Middle step: giving without knowing who gets it
Lowest step: giving with a frown
look.cite: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Gifts to the Poor 10:7–14 (c. 1180), retold in simple words
look.prompt: Why do you think helping someone earn their own is the best step?

check.q: What does tzedakah mean?
choices: Giving a share to people in need
check.why: Tzedakah is giving a share to people who need it. The word comes from a word for fair.

check.q: Who did the Talmud say gives tzedakah?
check.why: The Talmud (Gittin 7b) says even a poor person gives tzedakah.

check.q: What did Maimonides make?
check.why: Maimonides listed eight steps of giving, from lowest to best.

lessons.title: Feed the Animals First
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud says to feed your animals before you eat, because they cannot ask.
reading: Here is a small rule with a big heart. The Talmud says feed your *animals* before you sit down to eat. Your dog cannot open the fridge. Your goat cannot ask for hay.
The rabbis found this in a verse. The Torah says God gives grass for your cattle, and then you will eat. The grass comes first in the verse. The rabbis read that order as a rule.

Now you have read seven kindness rules. Each one helps someone. The sick person. The guest. The parent. The shamed person. The owner. The person in need. The hungry animal. The rabbis wrote rules to help them.

words.d: creatures in your care; the Talmud says to feed them before you eat

look.title: Who Does Each Rule Help?
look.text: Look at a table with seven cards. One card says Visit. One says Welcome. One says Honor. One says Do not shame. One says Bring it back. One says Give a share. One says Feed the animals. Under each card is a picture of a person or an animal.
look.prompt: Pick three cards. Say who each rule helps, and how you could do it this week.

check.q: When does the Talmud say to feed your animals?
check.why: The Talmud (Berakhot 40a) says to feed your animals before you sit down to eat.

check.q: Where did the rabbis find this rule?
choices: In a verse of the Torah
check.why: The rabbis read Deuteronomy 11:15, where grass for cattle comes before eating.

check.q: Who does the rule about lost things help?
check.why: Bringing a lost thing back helps the owner who lost it.

review.why: A mitzvah is a rule in the Torah. The rabbis also use it for a good deed.

review.q: Who ran to feed three strangers?
review.why: Genesis 18 says Abraham ran to the strangers and served them a meal.

review.q: What did Dama refuse to do?
review.why: The Talmud says Dama lost a sale rather than wake his father.

review.q: What does the owner give to get a lost thing back?
review.why: The Mishnah says the owner gives a sign, a secret detail only the owner knows.

review.q: What does the word tzedakah come from?
review.why: Tzedakah comes from a word for fair. The rabbis said giving is what is fair.

review.q: What did the rabbis compare shaming someone to?
review.why: The Talmud says a shamed face goes white, like a wound.
